title: A gasoline shock reverses some US household inflation and spending gaps
source_unit: New York Fed Economic Heterogeneity Indicator for demographic, economic, geographic, and income-group outcomes
geography: United States national indicators, with demographic, regional, urban/rural, and income-group comparisons

denominator.unit: major US metropolitan areas used in the demographic-CPI construction, with smaller places assigned by census region

hispanic_relative_direction.unit: direction of constructed demographic inflation gap in April 2026

low_middle_income_relative_direction.unit: direction of constructed demographic inflation gap in April 2026

high_income_relative_direction.unit: direction of constructed demographic inflation gap in April 2026

observations.method: Demographic expenditure shares from BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey microdata are combined with category and metro CPI inflation; group contributions are aggregated to demographic inflation indexes and compared with overall inflation.
observations.uncertainty: Demographic inflation is an author-constructed estimate, not an official BLS demographic CPI. It uses prior CEX expenditure shares, assumes common category prices within a metro, and uses urban prices for the rural comparison. The report attributes the reversal in part to gasoline prices after March 2026.
observations.subgroup: Race/ethnicity, income, education, age, census region, and urban/rural status.
observations.counterinterpretation: The reversal may reflect changing expenditure weights and assigned gasoline prices rather than a uniform price experience within a group; the indicator does not identify individual bills or policy causality.

denominator.unit: reported comparison benchmark for each earnings-ratio series

noncollege_to_college_earnings.unit: percent of workers with a college degree's earnings

observations.method: National EHI earnings ratios calculated for employed worker groups using BLS-based earnings measures; ratios compare group average earnings to a named benchmark.
observations.uncertainty: Ratios describe earnings among employed workers and do not capture differential employment, hours, occupation, or selection into work. The indicator is descriptive rather than a causal decomposition.
observations.counterinterpretation: Short-run ratio changes may reflect composition, hours, occupation, employment selection, or labor-market mix rather than a change in bargaining power alone.

denominator.unit: balanced Numerator household panel used for receipt-level retail spending indicators

real_gas_spending.unit: direction after March 2026 gasoline price shock

lower_income_real_gas_response.unit: relative direction of real gasoline consumption change

high_income_nominal_gas_spending.unit: relative direction of nominal gasoline spending change

real_retail_ex_auto.unit: direction after March 2026 gasoline price shock

observations.method: Receipt-level Numerator spending is aggregated by demographic group, deflated using demographic-specific inflation indexes, and seasonally adjusted; national retail excludes automobiles.
observations.uncertainty: The panel is a market-research receipt and permissioned-email source, not a government probability survey. Directional group trends do not establish a within-household causal effect of gasoline prices or distinguish quantity, substitution, and quality changes.
observations.subgroup: Income, education, race/ethnicity, age, urban status, and census region.
observations.counterinterpretation: Spending changes may reflect income, wealth, credit, commuting need, vehicle efficiency, employment, weather, or other contemporaneous shocks; nominal spending can rise while real consumption falls.

boundary: This record measures constructed demographic inflation, employed-worker earnings ratios, and aggregate receipt-based consumer-spending directions through April 2026. It does not establish individual price payment, household-specific gasoline exposure, policy causality, trust, political action, or a same-household cost-to-behavior chain. The EHI indicators are not official estimates of the Federal Reserve System or FOMC.
